title: don’t let AI take away the things that make us human #marjorieprime #...
transcript: Every single day AI Is getting smarter. It's learning how to sound like us and think like us. And because of this, Marjorie Prime feels less like SCI fi and more like a warning. But what makes this play so powerful is that at the center of all of this technology is something so deeply human. And that's 96-year-old June Squibb who brings a lifetime of lived experience to every moment on stage. She plays Marjorie, whose memory is beginning to fray. And because of this, she spends her days reminiscing with an AI Version of her late husband. He's called A prime. And he reminds her of the things she's forgotten. It's deeply unsettling and yet surprisingly tender. And June Squibb is absolutely luminous. She's so funny and vulnerable and commands the stage. And the cast around her is really, really affecting. With Cynthia Nixon, Christopher Lowell and Danny Burstein, who is particularly devastating. In a world increasingly shaped by AI Marjorie Prime reminds us that memory, grief and love are still deeply human. Technology might be able to store information or even memory, but it'll never be able to process the complicated, messy way we remember the people we love. And that's what makes this play so relevant. It doesn't just ask what the future looks like. It asks what we risk losing if we forget what makes us human in the first place.
